summary: Horisite ("Horizon + Site") is a free, browser-based interactive 3D explorer of the Moon's south pole designed to solve the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. At the lunar south pole, extreme topography means a distant ridge can block sunlight for power or sever direct line-ofsight communication with Earth. Horisite unifies complex ephemerides and real elevation data into a single intuitive interface. Users can select south pole candidate sites (such as Shackleton rim, Malapert massif, de Gerlache, Nobile, and Haworth), set any date and time, and visualize real NASA LRO/LOLA terrain at true scale alongside Sun and Earth horizon clearance margins, solar panel irradiance (W/m2), 24-hour visibility timelines, 30-day optimal mission windows, and a 15-stage Earth-to-Moon mission simulation.
details:
Horisite is an interactive web application designed to analyze sunlight conditions and Earth visibility in regions near the Moon’s south pole. Users can compare up to three locations, select a UTC date and time, adjust the observer’s height, and explore the lunar environment through three views: 3D terrain, surface, and lunar globe.

The system combines astronomical ephemerides with real elevation data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s LOLA instrument. For each location, it calculates the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth, including parallax, and compares them with the horizon created by the surrounding terrain. The application displays elevation, azimuth, horizon clearance, incident solar irradiance, and expected conditions over the next 24 hours. It can also search a 30-day period for the longest continuous window during which both the Sun and the center of Earth are visible from every selected location.

Using a selected window, users can explore an educational 13-stage Earth–Moon–Earth mission simulation, including launch, parking orbits, lunar travel, landing, surface stay, ascent, and return. Circular parking orbits use an analytical two-body model, while the transfers are clearly presented as illustrative visualizations rather than operational trajectories.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Horisite transforms complex scientific data into an accessible, visual, and reproducible experience. It helps students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts understand how lunar terrain can affect both sunlight availability and direct line of sight to Earth.

The project aims to increase interest in lunar exploration while encouraging critical thinking about the factors involved in selecting regions for future missions. It demonstrates that illumination, energy generation, communication, landing safety, and orbital feasibility are related but distinct engineering challenges.

Technologies Used

Horisite was developed using:

- HTML5, CSS3, and modern JavaScript;

- Three.js 0.186.1 and WebGL for 3D visualization;

- Astronomy Engine 2.1.19 for ephemerides and lunar orientation;

- Node.js for data preparation, automated testing, and the local server;

- GeoTIFF tools for processing digital elevation data;

- NASA LRO/LOLA terrain data and planetary textures;

- Git and GitHub for version control;

- automated validation and comparison with a JPL Horizons reference case.

The application is static and performs its calculations directly in the browser. It does not require external APIs during normal use or any specialized hardware—only a modern browser with WebGL support.

Creative Approach

Horisite’s creative strength is the integration of scientific analysis, interactive comparison, and mission storytelling. Instead of presenting only tables or a generic lunar globe, the application places users on real terrain, displays a 360-degree local horizon, and transforms a visibility window into a visual journey from Earth to the Moon and back.

The project also clearly distinguishes between measured data, physically calculated results, and illustrative elements. This creates an engaging experience without concealing the model’s scientific limitations.

Factors Considered by the Team

The team considered accuracy, transparency, performance, accessibility, reproducibility, and educational value. The model accounts for lunar curvature, observer height, parallax, terrain obstruction, the visible fraction of the solar disk, panel orientation, and temporal sampling.

The team also carefully documented what the application does not calculate. Horisite does not determine complete communications performance, electrical energy production, fuel consumption, delta-v, landing risk, or operational flight trajectories. Its locations are regional reference points rather than certified landing sites. These limitations are presented directly in the interface to promote responsible interpretation of the results.
